title: Eating and drinking
goal: Order food without nerves, talk about what you like, and learn how real Brazilians order — including habits that never make it into phrasebooks.
bekal: order with *eu quero*, *eu vou querer* and *para mim*
use *querer* and *poder* — two irregular verbs that open every request
say what you like and dislike with a sensible range of strength

notes: **Vou querer, not quero.** This habit separates beginners from people who've lived in Brazil. Ordering with *eu quero* ("I want") is correct but sounds a bit blunt, like a child making demands. The usual form is *vou querer* — literally "I'm going to want" — which sounds much softer, like English "I'll have". The form itself is explained in unit 11; for now, learn it whole as your ordering phrase.

**Pode deixar** literally means "you can leave it", and it means "leave it to me, consider it done". It's the typical Brazilian answer to any request, and you'll hear it from waiters, repairmen and friends alike. Closest English equivalent: "you got it" or "no problem".

**Você pode trazer…? is the most useful polite-request formula.** Literally "you can bring?", and Portuguese needs nothing extra to make it polite — no *would* or *could* to learn. Just *pode* + infinitive.
**Adoro, not gosto muito.** Brazilians use *adorar* ("to adore") for ordinary things: *Adoro café*, *Adoro esse filme*. To other ears it can sound over the top; in Brazil it's the normal measure.

**Já trago** = "I'll bring it right away". The word *já* means "already" **and** "right away", depending on the verb. It's one of the small words that come up most in Brazilian conversation: *Já vou* (I'm leaving now), *Já acabou?* (finished already?).

grammars.title: Querer and poder — two keys to every request
body: Two irregular verbs that open almost every polite sentence. Both are followed by a verb **in the infinitive**, with no change at all.
after: **The second verb doesn't change at all.** *Eu quero comer*, *Você pode ajudar*, *Nós queremos ir*. That's big news: a sentence needs only one conjugated verb, and the rest stays in its dictionary form. English works almost the same way (*I want to eat*), just without the *to*.
⚠️ Look at the form *quer* — no vowel at the end. It's said **kehh**, not "keh-reh". And *quero* is said **KEH-roo**, not "kweh-roh": the *u* after *q* is always silent before *e* and *i*.
To decline politely, use *não, obrigado* or *hoje não* ("not today") — both sound far friendlier than *não quero*, which comes across as curt.

grammars.title: Talking about tastes, from hate to love
body: Six levels, all used every day. Watch which ones need *de* and which don't.

head: Português
Needs de?
English
rows: I'm not a big fan of beer.

after: ⚠️ The first and last rows do **not** use *de*; the four in the middle must. The reason is simple: *adorar* and *odiar* are ordinary verbs, while *gostar* always demands *de*. Just remember that *gostar* is the odd one out, not the others.

**Row four is the polite way to turn down food.** *Não gosto muito de…* literally means "I don't like … very much", and in Brazil it's much gentler than *não gosto*. Handy when you're offered something you don't want at someone's home.

grammars.title: Com, sem, and para mim
body: Three little words that cover almost every ordering sentence.
after: ⚠️ **Para mim, not para eu.** After a preposition, Portuguese uses a special form: *mim* (me), *você* (you), *ele/ela* (him/her), *nós* (us). Only "I" changes form — just like English *I* → *me* — and it's the one used most, so learn *para mim* as a single chunk.
**Para viagem** literally means "for the trip", and it's how you say "to go" in Brazil. If you ask for *para levar*, you'll be understood too — but *para viagem* is what's written on the menu board.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *A conta* and *o cartão* meet in sentences you'll use every day: *A conta, por favor* and *No cartão, por favor*. In Brazil the waiter almost always brings the card machine to your table, so you don't need to get up.

blocks.text: **Cafezinho literally means "little coffee"**, and you need to recognize that **-inho** ending now: it adds a sense of small, friendly or affectionate to any word. *Um minutinho* (just a sec), *obrigadinho* (thanks a bunch), *amiguinho* (little buddy). Brazilians use it constantly, and it's one of the most distinctive features of their speech.

Turning down a *cafezinho* in a Brazilian home is seen as a little cold — like refusing a cup of tea when you visit someone's grandmother. If you don't drink coffee, a safe answer is: *Aceito um copo d'água, obrigado.*
